title: Milton to Los Angeles: The Comprehensive Anticipatory Design Science of a Single Individual
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Milton, Massachusetts, the birth house
stops.campa: In the old Unitarian town below the Blue Hills, Richard Buckminster Fuller is born on the twelfth of July into a New England lineage that has already spoken with the Over-Soul. His great-aunt is Margaret Fuller, editor of The Dial, who declared the universe herself and drowned off Fire Island; the family carries transcendentalism in its blood like a second surname. The boy is severely far-sighted, seeing the world only as blurred pools of color until spectacles at four years give him sudden, astonished edges. From that first correction he trusts the whole over the fragment.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Margaret Fuller, editor of The Dial

stops.name: Bear Island, Penobscot Bay, Maine, the summer place
stops.campa: Each summer the family crosses to Bear Island in Penobscot Bay, and here the boy becomes an engineer of necessity. Given no store of ready tools, he builds his own boats and jetties from what the tide brings, and one year invents a mechanical jellyfish-pushing oar: a human-powered propulsion he works out from watching the sea creatures pulse. On the guest register of the summer house he signs a different version of his name each year, trying the sound of himself. The island teaches him that nature builds with the fewest parts, always.

stops.name: Milton Academy, the Froebel table
stops.campa: At kindergarten and then Milton Academy, the near-blind boy is given the Froebel gifts: the little sticks and dried peas of the reform kindergarten. Asked to build a structure, the other children make cubes and houses; he, who cannot see well enough to copy the expected forms, feels for the shape that will not wobble and arrives, by touch, at the tetrahedron and the octet. The teacher is startled. Decades later he insists this blind fumbling at the pea-and-toothpick table was the true first sighting of the triangulated, self-bracing geometry that will become his life's whole grammar.
stops.quote: Nature is trying very hard to make us succeed, but nature does not depend on us. We are not the only experiment.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, recalling his kindergarten geometry (attributed, widely quoted)

stops.name: Harvard University, Cambridge, Adams House, twice cast out
stops.campa: The fifth generation of Fullers to enter Harvard arrives in the fall of 1913 and swiftly undoes himself. Overwhelmed, he draws out his whole term's allowance and squanders it in New York on a chorus troupe from the Ziegfeld Follies, entertaining an entire dance company on a single grand gesture. Harvard expels him for cutting classes and irresponsibility. Readmitted, he fails again, for what the college calls his lack of interest, and is expelled a second time. He never takes a degree. The most-lectured man of the coming century leaves the university certified in nothing.

stops.name: Sherbrooke, Quebec, the cotton mill
stops.campa: Cast out, he goes north to a Canadian textile mill as an apprentice millwright, learning the machinery from the shaft up, fitting and installing the imported looms. Here the transcendentalist's grandnephew acquires the other half of himself: the hands of a mechanic, the reverence for the well-made bearing and the true tolerance. He will forever hold that the engineer and the poet are one worker, and that a man who cannot dress a machine has no right to dream about civilization. The mill floor is his second university, and this one he does not fail.

stops.name: USS Inca / Bay Shore Naval Air Station, Long Island, the crash-boat commander
stops.campa: The Great War takes him into the U.S. Navy, where the fumbling scholar finds his element. He commands a crash-rescue boat flotilla, pulling downed aviators from the water, and invents a winch-and-mast rig that can lift a sunken seaplane out fast enough to save the trapped pilot's life. The Navy sends him to Annapolis for officer training. From the sea service he takes a lifelong vision: the ship as a total system, self-contained, that must carry everything it needs, the seed of the phrase he will one day give the whole planet, Spaceship Earth.

stops.name: Rock Hall, Lawrence, Long Island, the wedding to Anne Hewlett
stops.campa: On his twenty-second birthday he marries Anne Hewlett, daughter of the architect James Monroe Hewlett, and binds himself to a partner who will hold the ground of his life for sixty-six years. Through Anne's father he first meets a building system worth improving; through Anne herself he gains the still centre without which none of the coming ruin and glory could be survived. The marriage is not an episode but the constant of the whole journey. She is present at the water's edge, present at every dome, and present, comatose, at the very end.

segments.name: The Ruin and the Water's Edge

stops.name: New York City, the death of Alexandra
stops.campa: His first daughter Alexandra, born in the influenza winter, is a fragile, uncannily perceptive child. Just before her fourth birthday she dies of complications of polio and spinal meningitis, in Fuller's arms. He is convinced the damp, cold, ill-made housing of the age has killed her: that shelter itself, badly done, is lethal. The grief does not release him; it becomes a life's charge. Everything he will later build to house humanity cheaply, drily, warmly, is a father's argument with the death of one small girl.

stops.name: Manhattan, the Dymaxion Chronofile begins its daily record
stops.campa: From the year of his turning he keeps the Dymaxion Chronofile: the most exhaustive documentation of a single human life ever attempted. Every letter received and sent, every bill, sketch, clipping, doodle and note is pasted into the running ledger; from 1920 he claims to log his days at intervals as fine as fifteen minutes. It grows to some two hundred seventy feet of paper, a self as a laboratory notebook, the one experimental subject observed without pause for sixty years. He treats his own life as data offered to the future.
stops.quote: I made up my mind... to be the most rigorously documented human being in history.

stops.name: Stockade Building System, the collapse of the enterprise
stops.campa: With his father-in-law he has built the Stockade Building System, lightweight fibrous compressed blocks for cheap, weatherproof houses, and put himself, undegreed and unmoneyed, at its head. Some two hundred forty houses go up. Then the investors sell the firm out from under him and he is dismissed as president in 1927, penniless, jobless, with a newborn second daughter, Allegra, just arrived. The reformer of shelter is himself without secure shelter, thirty-two years old and, by every worldly measure, a failure.

stops.name: The shore of Lake Michigan, Chicago, the night on the edge
stops.campa: On an autumn night, ruined and drinking, living in low-income rooms on the North Side, he walks out to the edge of Lake Michigan resolved to drown himself, reasoning his life insurance is worth more to Anne and Allegra than he is. At the water's brink he is stopped. He feels himself lifted from the ground, wrapped in a sphere of white light, and a voice speaks with authority he cannot doubt: he does not have the right to eliminate himself; he does not belong to himself; he need never again await the world's approval of his thought. He does not go into the water.
stops.quote: From now on you need never await temporal attestation to your thought. You think the truth. You do not have the right to eliminate yourself. You do not belong to you. You belong to Universe.
stops.quote_source: Fuller's account of the Lake Michigan voice, recounted in Ideas and Integrities (1963) and in his lectures

stops.name: Chicago, the year of silence and the vow
stops.campa: Turned back from death, he takes a private vow the size of the age: he will resign the ordinary earning of a living and instead conduct a fifty-year experiment, offering himself as a single, unfunded human guinea pig, to find and prove what one individual can do on behalf of all humanity that great institutions and governments cannot or will not do. To think clearly he stops talking almost entirely for the better part of two years, a self-imposed silence to burn out the borrowed words and hear only what is true. When he speaks again, the language is his own.
stops.quote: What is it on this planet that needs doing that I know something about, that probably won't happen unless I take responsibility for it?
stops.quote_source: Fuller's formulation of his 1927 vow (widely attributed)

stops.name: Greenwich Village, New York, Romany Marie's café and the 4D house
stops.campa: He surfaces in Greenwich Village, decorating Romany Marie's bohemian café in exchange for meals and the right to hold forth. Here, hanging a model of a hexagonal house slung from a single central mast, he draws crowds; here the young sculptor Isamu Noguchi, sent by Brancusi, becomes his friend and collaborator. He calls the design 4D: the fourth dimension, time, a mass-producible dwelling machine that generates its own power and manages its own waste. When Marshall Field's exhibits the model, an adman blends the syllables of his talk into a single trademark: Dymaxion, dynamic, maximum, tension.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, from the 4D / Dymaxion period writings

stops.name: Philadelphia, Shelter magazine and 'Nine Chains to the Moon'
stops.campa: Through the deepest Depression he edits and largely writes the little magazine Shelter, preaching that housing must be reconceived as a mass-produced industrial service, not a hand-laid craft. Out of these years comes his first book, Nine Chains to the Moon, whose title measures the 1938 human race: stood one on another's shoulders, the population would bridge to the moon nine times over. Einstein himself blesses the manuscript, telling the young man his account of relativity is sound. In forty-three leaping chapters Fuller coins ephemeralization: the trend of doing ever more with ever less.
suggested_refs: Nine Chains to the Moon, first edition 1938

stops.name: Bridgeport, Connecticut, Tongue Point, the Dymaxion car
stops.campa: In the shuttered Locomobile plant at Tongue Point, on the very day Roosevelt closes the banks, he founds the Dymaxion Corporation and with the naval architect Starling Burgess and twenty-seven mechanics builds a streamlined, three-wheeled land craft: teardrop-bodied, front-wheel-driven, rear-steered, able to turn in its own length and carry eleven. It is aircraft thinking brought to the road, a decade before its time. Three prototypes rise from the old dynamometer hall. Amelia Earhart and H. G. Wells come to ride in it; the newsreels swarm.

stops.name: Chicago, the Century of Progress crash
stops.campa: Almost at the gates of the Century of Progress World's Fair, Dymaxion Prototype One rolls over at speed. Its driver, Francis Turner, is killed; two distinguished passengers are hurt. A rival car had crowded it off the road, but the press reports only the death-trap with three wheels, and the investors flee. Fuller pours in his own inheritance to finish the second and third cars, then must sell them all and dissolve the corporation. The land-going aircraft is buried under a headline. He keeps the geometry and lets the machine go.

stops.name: New York, the Dymaxion Map in Life magazine
stops.campa: In the depths of the world war he unfolds the globe. His Dymaxion map projects the sphere onto an icosahedron and lays it flat with almost no distortion of size or shape, and, crucially, with no top and no bottom, no privileged north, no centre and margin. Life magazine prints it as a cut-out the reader can fold back into a solid. Here is his politics made geometry: one island Earth, one nearly-continuous continent of humanity, no nation naturally above another. He asks the reader to hold the whole planet in two hands at once.
stops.quote: There is no 'up' and 'down' in Universe. The words are meaningless.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, on the Dymaxion map and Universe
suggested_refs: Dymaxion Air-Ocean World Map, Life magazine 1943

stops.name: Wichita, Kansas, the Dymaxion Dwelling Machine
stops.campa: With the war's surplus of aluminium and idle bomber lines, Beech Aircraft in Wichita takes up his round, mast-hung Dymaxion Dwelling Machine: a four-ton house wringing weight from an aircraft's habits, self-ventilating through a rotating vent-cap, air-shippable, mass-producible. Two prototypes rise; tens of thousands of orders are said to wait. Then he will not release it before it is perfected to his own standard, quarrels with the board over readiness, and resigns. The one house that might have housed millions never goes into production. A single surviving unit becomes a museum relic.
suggested_refs: Dymaxion House, The Henry Ford museum, Dearborn

stops.name: Black Mountain College, North Carolina, the supine dome and the disciples
stops.campa: Josef Albers calls him to Black Mountain College in the summer of 1948, into the same season as John Cage, Merce Cunningham and de Kooning. He gathers venetian-blind slats to raise a great geodesic hemisphere; warning in advance that the metal is too weak, he raises it anyway and it folds gently to the grass: the supine dome, a failure he blesses as data. He acts in Cage's staging of Satie. Returning in 1949 to direct the summer, he and his twelve student 'disciples' at last stand a true self-supporting geodesic dome. The sphere from struts is born.
stops.quote: There is nothing in a caterpillar that tells you it's going to be a butterfly.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, from the Black Mountain years (attributed)

stops.name: Raleigh, North Carolina, Geodesics Inc. and the tensegrity
stops.campa: In Raleigh he founds Geodesics Inc. and works out, with his students, the principle he names tensegrity, tensional integrity, in which a scatter of compression struts float, touching nowhere, inside a continuous net of tension, so that the whole holds together the way the taut universe does, by pull rather than by pile. The dome is its child: a sphere assembled from triangles that grows stronger and lighter the larger it becomes, the only human structure whose strength rises with its size. The Marine Corps orders domes it can drop by helicopter.
stops.quote: Tensegrity describes a structural-relationship principle in which structural shape is guaranteed by the finitely closed, comprehensively continuous, tensional behaviors of the system.
suggested_refs: Geodesics Inc. Marine Corps airlift domes

stops.name: Dearborn, Michigan, the Ford Rotunda dome
stops.campa: The Ford Motor Company wants to roof the round court of its Rotunda, and its engineers say the old walls cannot bear a conventional dome of the span required. Fuller drapes the whole court with a geodesic of aluminium struts weighing a fraction of what steel would, eight and a half tons spanning ninety-three feet, and it stands. The first commercial geodesic dome makes the doubters into believers overnight. The impossible, made almost weightless, becomes ordinary. Industry begins ordering domes by the hundred; the patent of 1954 secures the invention.
stops.quote: When I am working on a problem, I never think about beauty... but when I have finished, if the solution is not beautiful, I know it is wrong.

stops.name: Kabul, Afghanistan, the airlifted domes of the trade fairs
stops.campa: The United States sends his golden geodesic domes abroad as ambassadors, flown into the international trade fairs at Kabul and elsewhere on the far side of the earth, raised in days, dazzling the crowds. A shape born from near-blind kindergarten sticks now lands, folded in an aircraft, in a Central Asian capital and unfolds into a pavilion larger than a great tent. The dome is the most efficient enclosure of space humanity has found, and it travels the globe as proof that his half-forgotten geometry has become a working tool of nations.
stops.quote: You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.

stops.name: Carbondale, Illinois, the dome home and Southern Illinois University
stops.campa: At Southern Illinois University he is made research professor of design science, and on 407 South Forest Avenue he raises, in a single seven-hour morning, the one geodesic dome he will ever live in and the only house he will ever own. Here, with Anne, in the years 1960 to 1971, he writes eleven books, is granted nine patents, and designs the Montreal sphere. From this small hemisphere in southern Illinois the ceaseless world-circling begins in earnest; he sets out from the dome and returns to it between orbits of the planet.
suggested_refs: R. Buckminster Fuller and Anne Hewlett Dome Home, Carbondale

stops.name: Montreal, Île Sainte-Hélène, the Biosphère at Expo 67
stops.campa: For Expo 67 he crowns the United States Pavilion with a three-quarter geodesic sphere two hundred fifty feet across and twenty stories high: a double-layered lattice of steel tubes skinned in acrylic that mirrors the sun by day and glows from within by night. Millions pass through what he calls a skybreak bubble, a piece of controlled sky. Years later a chemist, remembering this dome, gives the newly found spherical carbon molecule the name buckminsterfullerene, the buckyball, so that his geometry is written into the atoms themselves.
stops.quote: I am a passenger on the spaceship, Earth.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth

stops.name: Carbondale / New York, Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth
stops.campa: He publishes Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth and gives the age its governing image: the planet is a vessel travelling sixty thousand miles an hour through the universe, carrying no instruction manual, its energy income all sunlight, its crew obliged to run it as a single closed system for everybody or nobody. There are, he insists, no passengers on Spaceship Earth: only crew. Wealth is not gold but the organized know-how to do more and more with less and less, until we can sustain all humanity at a higher standard than any have known. The word ephemeralization is his.
stops.quote: We are not going to be able to operate our Spaceship Earth successfully nor for much longer unless we see it as a whole spaceship and our fate as common. It has to be everybody or nobody.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth (1969)
suggested_refs: Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, first edition

stops.name: New York, the World Game on the Dymaxion Map
stops.campa: He lays his no-top-no-bottom Dymaxion map out huge upon a floor and invites players to walk across the whole earth's resources at once, and play the World Game: not the war-games of the general staffs, which ask how to win a nation's advantage, but a global game whose only winning condition is to make the world work for one hundred percent of humanity in the shortest time, through spontaneous cooperation, without ecological offense or the disadvantage of anyone. He treats scarcity as a design failure, not a law of nature, and asks the young to redesign the whole system.
stops.quote: Make the world work, for 100% of humanity, in the shortest possible time, through spontaneous cooperation, without ecological offense or the disadvantage of anyone.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, the World Game challenge

stops.name: New Delhi, the Nehru Memorial Lecture
stops.campa: The world-circler comes to India: one of forty-eight orbits of the planet, part of a hundred globe-girdling tours delivering thousands of lectures at five hundred universities. Invited to give the Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Lecture in the capital of Indira Gandhi's India, he unrolls Spaceship Earth before a nation of half a billion crew members. He befriends the Delhi architects, walks the zoo with Joseph Stein, and presses his gospel that poverty is a solvable design problem, that there is enough for all if the world is run as one integrated system. The old empires' map, he says, is obsolete.
stops.quote: We are called to be architects of the future, not its victims.
suggested_refs: Fuller and Joseph Stein, Delhi Zoo, 1969

stops.name: Philadelphia, 'I Seem to Be a Verb' and the ceaseless circling
stops.campa: Now the most-travelled lecturer on earth, he circles the globe again and again, keeping several days' worth of time zones in his pockets at once, sleeping in the Dymaxion snatches he prescribes. He declares himself not a noun but a verb, not a thing but an unfolding process, an integral function of the universe. He wants no monument; he asks that his epitaph read only Call Me Trimtab, after the little tab on a ship's rudder that, with the least possible force, turns the whole great vessel around. One individual, rightly placed, moves the world.
stops.quote: I am not a thing — a noun. I seem to be a verb, an evolutionary process — an integral function of the universe.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, I Seem to Be a Verb (1970)
suggested_refs: I Seem to Be a Verb, first edition
'Call Me Trimtab' gravestone, Mount Auburn Cemetery

stops.name: Philadelphia, 'Everything I Know,' the forty-two-hour testament
stops.campa: At eighty he sits before the cameras and speaks, over some forty-two recorded hours, everything he knows, a whole cosmology delivered from memory without notes: the geometry of the universe, the history of industrialization, synergetics, the story of his own turning at the water. It is the summa of the fifty-year experiment, filmed so nothing will be lost. In the same span he pours his life's mathematics into the two vast volumes of Synergetics, the geometry of thinking, insisting that nature computes only in whole numbers and closest-packed spheres, never in the fictions of the plane.
stops.quote: Synergy is the only word in our language that means behavior of whole systems unpredicted by the separately observed behaviors of any of the system's separate parts.

stops.name: Washington, D.C., the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stops.campa: The undegreed man twice expelled from Harvard, ruined at thirty-two, is given the nation's highest civilian honour. President Reagan awards him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the citation calls him a true Renaissance man and one of the greatest minds of the age, whose contributions as geometrician, educator and architect-designer are benchmarks of accomplishment. The verb has been recognized. He is eighty-seven; the fifty-year experiment he began at the water's edge is very nearly run, and the single individual has, by any measure, done a great deal for humanity.
stops.quote: The things to do are: the things that need doing, that you see need to be done, and that no one else seems to see need to be done.

stops.name: Los Angeles, Good Samaritan Hospital, the two deaths
stops.campa: In Los Angeles his wife Anne lies comatose, dying of cancer. On the first of July he sits at her bedside, and after sixty-six years of marriage he suddenly cries out that she is squeezing his hand. Then he rises, is struck by a heart attack, and dies within the hour at Good Samaritan Hospital, eleven days short of his eighty-eighth birthday. Anne, never waking, follows him thirty-six hours later. They are carried home together to Mount Auburn in Cambridge, back to the transcendentalist ground he came from, under a stone that reads, as he asked, Call Me Trimtab.
stops.quote_source: R. Buckminster Fuller, his chosen epitaph, Mount Auburn Cemetery, Cambridge
